t: Why Detachment Is A Powerful Classroom Management Strategy management-strategy/
q: They view the profession as who they are rather than what they do.
It steals from students the gift of responsibility, causing learned helplessness, boredom, dissatisfaction, and, ultimately, more misbehavior.
The most effective teachers, on the other hand, maintain a level of detachment from the job.
They know that if they care too much, if they allow themselves to be pulled in too deep, then it will cloud their judgment.
It gives them perspective, impartiality, and wisdom along with strong leadership presence.
For many teachers, this one change, this small tweak in emotional and physical distance, can be monumental, both in enjoyment of the job and effectiveness.
x: Linsin argues that teachers who struggle most with classroom management tend to be overly emotionally invested, treating teaching as an identity rather than a job and getting pulled into constant one-on-one…
Over-investment pulls teachers into constant micromanagement, which causes learned helplessness and misbehavior in students.
Effective teachers maintain healthy emotional distance, building relationships through trust and consistency rather than personal enmeshment.

t: How To Eliminate Cell Phone Use In The Classroom sroom/
q: Unless your content and ability to deliver it are more compelling than the highly addictive nature of cell phones, then learning will be profoundly and negatively affected.
Merely banning their use doesn’t go far enough and will only lead to arguing and battling with students over what, exactly, this means.
As for consequences, I recommend that phones be taken away without students first receiving a warning. Otherwise, they’ll use up their warning every chance they get.
By using a plastic bag rather than taking the phone by hand, it shows respect for the student’s property.
Everyone must buy in. Every teacher and administrator on campus must follow the policy as it’s written in the student handbook. Otherwise, it isn’t worth the paper it’s printed on.
It will work anywhere and at any school that commits to it and decides that enough is enough.
x: Prompted by watching A&E's Undercover High, Linsin lays out a detailed, school-wide policy for eliminating cell phone use in class, arguing that vague rules merely discouraging phone use are functionally meaningless.
Vague policies merely discouraging cell phone use are functionally meaningless and unenforceable.

His policy bans phones (and visible headphones) from even being pulled out between the start and end of class, with no gray area or exceptions based on intent, and recommends immediate confiscation without a prior…
Confiscation should happen immediately without a prior warning, using a ziplock bag as a respectful, non-confrontational method.
Uniform, school-wide teacher and administrator buy-in is essential; a policy followed by only some staff quickly loses credibility.

t: How To Drastically Improve Your Class
q: If ever your students aren’t giving you what you want . . . Stop them in their tracks. Reteach your expectations. Begin again.
Trotting it out every once in a while—or even more often than not—is not only confusing to students, but it sends the message that you don’t really mean what you say.
The strategy works because it forces you, as a natural consequence, to become extraordinarily effective with your initial instruction.
Your students may be so used to half listening, or not listening at all, that you'll have to repeat nearly everything you do.
Your students will realize that when you give an instruction, when you teach and model what you want in explicit detail, or just make a simple request, you really do mean for them to follow it.
It starts with an all-or-nothing commitment to mean what you say, to make your actions congruent with your words.
x: A simple, consistently applied secret—stop, reteach, begin again whenever expectations aren't met—can dramatically improve a class.
He explains that the strategy only works when applied consistently every single time, since inconsistent use confuses students and signals that the teacher doesn't mean what they say.
Commitment to the approach forces teachers to become more effective at initial instruction, not just more strict with consequences.

Linsin shares what he calls a secret known only to a small percentage of teachers despite its simplicity: whenever students fail to meet expectations, stop them immediately, reteach the expectation, and begin again.

t: Why It's Okay To Be Weird
q: It doesn’t mean you must dampen your enthusiasm or become a robot when you step in front of your students.
Students are drawn to uniqueness, to teachers who are unabashedly themselves. They want to be around them, learn from them, and follow where they lead.
There is no passion in trying to be someone you’re not. You can fake it, but there will always be something missing.
Students don’t trust teachers who put on a show of perfection in their demeanor, manner, tone, and style.
It’s not uncommon for bright, funny, lovely people to change drastically the moment the morning bell rings.
Just being you, on the other hand, embracing your weird and wonderful self, unapologetically, is your greatest strength.
x: Linsin argues that staying calm as a teacher does not mean suppressing one's natural personality, and that embracing one's quirks and idiosyncrasies actually makes teachers more effective.
Students are drawn to genuine uniqueness and find over-controlled, stoic teachers less interesting and less engaging.

Students sense manufactured perfection as dishonest, which undermines trust even when the demeanor seems polished.

He observes that many naturally funny, warm people change dramatically the moment the school day begins, adopting a cold perfectionism that may suppress misbehavior but forecloses a genuinely happy classroom culture.
